extracted.intended_audience: recipients of Federal financial assistance (K-12 and postsecondary institutions), Title IX coordinators, school administrators, and legal/compliance counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying the Title IX regulatory definition of hostile-environment sex-based harassment by assessing fact-specific factors to determine whether unwelcome sex-based conduct is subjectively and objectively offensive and so severe or pervasive that it limits or denies access to an education program or activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality of the circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the 'constellation of surrounding circumstances, expectations, and relationships' (Oncale/Davis); consider the nature, frequency, and context of the conduct when determining whether conduct creates a hostile environment in a particular context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretations from Title VII and court precedent inform Title IX application. The list of factors in the regulation is not exhaustive; determinations require a fact-specific, totality-of-the-circumstances analysis. Examples are illustrative only and do not substitute for a case-specific inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of hostile environment sex-based harassment (legal standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hostile environment sex-based harassment is unwelcome sex-based conduct that is subjectively and objectively offensive and so severe or pervasive that it limits or denies a person's ability to participate in or benefit from the recipient's education program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal standard is not whether conduct is merely 'annoying' or 'immature'; it requires both subjective offensiveness (the complainant experienced it as unwelcome) and objective offensiveness (reasonable person standard) plus an effect on access/participation. Administrative enforcement standards need not be identical to the higher damages-liability standard from Davis.

rubrics_metrics.name: First factor — Degree of impact on complainant's access
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the degree to which the conduct affected the complainant's ability to access the recipient's education program or activity (access includes the ability to participate in or benefit from the program).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This must be an individualized, fact-specific analysis focused on the complainant; recipients should not evaluate based on a notion of a 'perfect victim.' Consideration of impacts on other community members is appropriate, but the first factor properly examines the effect on the particular complainant. Title IX Coordinators may initiate grievance procedures based on risk, pattern, or information suggesting broader impact even absent multiple complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second factor — Type, frequency, and duration of conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the type of conduct and its frequency and duration to inform whether conduct is severe and/or pervasive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although overlapping with 'severe or pervasive,' explicit reference to type/frequency/duration helps decisionmakers (e.g., consider both how often incidents occur and how long each incident lasted). A single request for a date or single gift 'generally' would not be pervasive, but fact-specific analysis is required before reaching conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third factor — Parties' ages, roles, prior interactions, and other relevant party-specific factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the ages and roles of the parties, prior interactions between them, and other factors about each party (including developmental levels or disabilities) that may be relevant to evaluating the effects of the conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This factor recognizes differing applicability across elementary/secondary and postsecondary contexts (e.g., power dynamics when student and employee involved). 'Other factors' is intended to include developmental level and disability-related considerations. The regulatory text was clarified to remove redundant wording (deleted 'alleged' and 'unwelcome' in that clause).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourth factor — Location and context of the conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess where and in what context the conduct occurred (e.g., school bus, dorm room, public space) because location and context affect intimidation, threat, humiliation, and the effect on access to programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Location/context informs unwelcomeness, objective offensiveness, and severity/pervasiveness. Because this factor covers relevant considerations, language referencing the recipient's 'control over the respondent' was removed to avoid conflation with Davis's damages-liability standard; recipients should use §106.11 discussion for issues of control over respondents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fifth factor — Other sex-based harassment in the recipient's program or activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether other sex-based harassment exists in the recipient's education program or activity and whether a pattern or multiple instances against the same person (or multiple people) make the conduct relevant to the hostile-environment analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a fact-specific inquiry: a single one-off remark may be insufficient, but repeated similar conduct by multiple peers over time (e.g., repeatedly calling a student 'girly') may create a hostile environment. A respondent's past harassment of others is not part of whether current conduct created a hostile environment for the complainant, though pattern evidence may be admissible in grievance procedures if objectively relevant to the allegations under investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online harassment — equivalence to in-person conduct when within program/activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Online conduct can constitute sex-based harassment if, based on the totality of the circumstances, it is unwelcome, subjectively and objectively offensive, and so severe or pervasive that it limits or denies access to the education program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must evaluate online conduct using the same factors as in-person conduct. Examples include sex-based derogatory name-calling, nonconsensual distribution of intimate images (including authentic and AI‑generated), cyberstalking, and sending sex-based pictures or cartoons. Recipients are not expected to monitor students' online activity outside their programs; but when a recipient has information that online conduct created a hostile environment in its program/activity, it must address it. The Department also explains K-12 schools retain authority to regulate some off-campus online speech under Mahanoy and subsequent case law, subject to First Amendment limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex stereotyping and gender identity as protected bases for harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: Harassment based on sex stereotypes (e.g., expectations about how boys/girls should act) or on gender identity can constitute sex-based harassment under Title IX if it meets the hostile-environment elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include statements like 'girls don't belong in school' or targeting students for failing to meet masculine stereotypes. Misgendering can be harassment depending on the facts, but a stray remark or a single misuse of language ordinarily will not suffice. The Department recognizes First Amendment concerns and notes nothing in the regulations requires violating free-speech protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrative examples, non-exhaustiveness, and limits on regulatory text
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples provided in the preamble and NPRM are illustrative only and not exhaustive; determination requires fuller fact-specific analysis and the regulatory factors are intentionally non-exhaustive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declines to opine definitively on hypotheticals in the preamble since a final determination requires investigation and evaluation of relevant facts. The regulatory definition intentionally does not limit consideration to listed factors due to the fact-specific nature of hostile-environment analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability in elementary and secondary school contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: The hostile-environment definition is applicable to K-12 settings and is intended to be workable, requiring administrators' judgment and accounting for parties' ages and objective offensiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Title IX obligations apply to elementary/secondary recipients; agencies have authority to define regulatory obligations as conditions of federal funding. The Department rejects the claim that the definition prevents judgment calls by school officials; elements like parties' ages and objective offensiveness narrow implicated conduct. Davis's higher damages-liability standard does not preclude administrative enforcement; schools have applied totality-of-circumstances assessments historically.
